passage:
Trisha, you're about to sign for that flat because they came down from thirty to twenty-six? Wait. Let your Seema maasi tell you something.

When I was twenty-four I wanted to buy a sewing machine for my tailoring work, a big industrial one. The first shop said eighty thousand. The owner smiled and said, "For you, seventy." I nearly paid. Seventy felt like a gift.

On the bus home, I asked myself: if I had never heard eighty, what would I think seventy was? I had no idea. That was the frightening part.

So the next week I visited two other shops in Surat and asked a tailor friend what she had paid. The same machine was fifty-five, fifty-eight, and she'd got hers for fifty-two.

I bought it for fifty-five. So, beta, before you sign, who else have you asked?

qa.q: What did the first shop say the sewing machine cost?
qa.a: The first shop said eighty thousand.

qa.q: What did young Seema feel when she realised she had no idea what seventy was worth?
qa.a: Young Seema felt frightened, because seventy had felt like a gift only because of the eighty she had just heard.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Seema's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking on the bus what she would think without the first figure, then checking two other shops and a friend, gave her independent comparisons to decide from.

qa.q: How might the first shop owner have seen young Seema's visit?
qa.a: The owner probably expected an easy sale, since offering seventy after eighty makes the lower price feel generous.

grounding: An elder recalls asking what she would think without the first price and gathering independent comparisons before buying.

The school's annual trip to Pelling was in three days, and the internet in the Gangtok office had been down since morning. Pema, the school's young admin officer, had one bus quote on her desk from Baljeet's travels: ninety-five thousand.

Baljeet phoned. "For the school, I'll make it eighty-five. But confirm today."

Eighty-five sounded reasonable next to ninety-five. Pema almost said yes. Then she stopped herself. If I'd never seen ninety-five, would eighty-five look right?

She honestly didn't know. So she walked to the post office, which had a phone line that worked, and called two other operators and the principal of a nearby school that had done the same trip last year.

The quotes were sixty-eight and seventy-two. The other school had paid seventy.

At four, she called Baljeet back. "Our range is seventy. Can you match it?" After a long pause, he said yes.

qa.q: Where did Pema walk to make phone calls?
qa.a: She walked to the post office, which had a phone line that worked.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she almost said yes to eighty-five?
qa.a: Pema felt relieved and tempted, since eighty-five sounded reasonable next to ninety-five, but then uneasy that she didn't really know.

qa.q: What steps did Pema take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Pema asked what she would think without the first figure, then got two other quotes and one school's past price, so her decision rested on independent comparisons.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt during the long pause?
qa.a: Baljeet may have felt caught off guard and a little disappointed, knowing his first figure no longer set the terms.

grounding: Under time pressure and a broken connection, a young administrator resets her reference point by gathering independent quotes.

Zainab had been freelancing as an illustrator for eight months when Damini, who ran a small publishing house in Hyderabad, emailed her: "We'd love you for our children's book. We can offer twelve thousand for the full set of drawings."

Twelve thousand felt like a lot. It was more than her last job. Zainab's hand hovered over the reply button.

Then she sat back. What would I think this job was worth if Damini had never mentioned a number?

She counted the pages: twenty-four illustrations, full colour. She messaged three illustrators she knew from art school and asked, honestly, what they would charge for that. She also checked the rates page of an illustrators' association.

The answers came back: thirty, thirty-five, twenty-eight. The association's range was similar.

Zainab wrote back politely, explaining the scope and suggesting thirty. Damini replied the next day: "Fair. Let's talk at twenty-eight?"

qa.q: How many illustrations did the children's book need?
qa.a: Twenty-four illustrations, full colour.

qa.q: Why did twelve thousand first feel like a lot to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab felt pleased and tempted because it was more than her last job, and she had no other figure to compare it with yet.

qa.q: What could another freelancer learn from how Zainab replied?
qa.a: Before answering, ask what the work is worth without the first figure, then check two or three independent sources like peers and an association.

It was Holi, and Jaya had to take the gujiyas to Charu's house before the colours started. The quickest way was down the lane with the brown dog.

Last night, her cousin had told a story about a boy whose leg was bitten so badly he needed twenty stitches. Jaya had dreamed about it.

Now she stood at the corner with the plate. The brown dog lay in the sun, tail thumping. Jaya's heart hammered. All dogs bite. That's what dogs do.

The long way would take twenty minutes.

Charu's grandmother saw her from the balcony. "Jaya! Moti won't hurt you. He's been here ten years and never bitten anyone."

Jaya didn't move. Ten years felt smaller than twenty stitches.

passage:
Friday night

Didn't sign up for the inter-school fest in Mumbai. Zeenat is going. Everyone is going. I told Ma I had a stomach ache.

The truth: I can't stop watching those videos. Trains packed with people hanging out the doors. A car flipping on the expressway. A bus in the rain. My feed is full of them, maybe twenty a day. Every time I open my phone there's another one.

So in my head, travelling to Mumbai = accident.

Zeenat laughed at me. She said, "Kamal, my Chacha has taken that train every day for eleven years. Nothing happened." I said he was lucky.

But now writing this I'm thinking. Twenty videos a day. From the whole country. Maybe from the whole world. And my feed keeps showing them because I keep watching them.

Maybe the trains aren't more dangerous. Maybe my phone just is.

qa.q: How many accident videos a day does Kamal say the feed shows?
qa.a: Maybe twenty a day.

qa.q: Why does Kamal feel that travelling to Mumbai means an accident?
qa.a: Kamal feels anxious because the feed keeps showing crash videos, so the danger seems everywhere even though the clips come from the whole country.

qa.q: What could Kamal try to get a truer picture of the risk?
qa.a: Kamal could stop watching the clips for a while and ask an adult or look up how many people travel that route safely every day.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Kamal's decision to skip the fest?
qa.a: Zeenat probably finds it surprising and a bit sad, since her Chacha has taken that train for eleven years without trouble.

grounding: A teenager who watches many viral accident clips believes travel is far riskier than it is and skips a school trip.

In Rekha's small town near Satara, everyone said she was the brightest girl in Class 11. Her maths teacher had arranged a scholarship at a coaching centre in Pune.

Rekha said no.

Her friend Madhuri found her behind the family's grocery shop, scrolling. "Why?"

Rekha held up the phone. A clip of a crowded Pune road. A chain-snatching caught on camera. A scooter crash at night. "Every day there's something. The city is dangerous."

"How many of these have you watched?"

"Hundreds, maybe."

"And how many girls from our school are studying in Pune right now?"

Rekha counted. Nine. Madhuri's own sister was one of them.

"Has anything happened to any of them?"

"No, but..."

"So hundreds of clips, and nine real girls who are fine."

Rekha put the phone face down on the rice sacks. She still felt the fear in her stomach. But for the first time, she wondered where it had really come from.

qa.a: Nine.

qa.a: Rekha felt afraid because she had watched hundreds of clips of accidents and chain-snatching, so seeing them often felt like they happen often.

qa.a: Rekha could talk to the nine girls in Pune, including Madhuri's sister, and discuss real safety steps with her teacher and family.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' block

Madhuri, second year, has an internship in Chennai next month. Her parents booked her a flight. She asked me to help her change it to a thirty-hour train journey, because of "all those crashes on the news". She had watched coverage of a plane crash abroad late into the night and could describe it in detail.

The same evening, I saw her ride out of the gate on her scooter without a helmet, to buy snacks. I stopped her. She laughed: "It's just five minutes."

I asked her to sit with me. We talked about how the crash she watched was one event, shown hundreds of times, while scooter accidents on our own road rarely make the news but happen far more often. She was quiet for a bit.

She agreed to wear her helmet every time, and to talk to her parents before changing anything about the flight.

Tejas, warden

qa.q: How long was the train journey Madhuri wanted instead of the flight?
qa.a: A thirty-hour train journey.

qa.q: Why did flying feel more frightening to Madhuri than riding without a helmet?
qa.a: Madhuri felt scared of flying because the dramatic crash coverage was vivid in her mind, while the everyday scooter ride felt familiar and safe.

qa.q: Why was Tejas's conversation a good countermeasure?
qa.a: Tejas calmly compared one crash shown many times with frequent local scooter accidents, and got a concrete promise: helmet every time.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's parents react when she talks to them?
qa.a: Madhuri's parents might feel relieved she is wearing a helmet and reassure her about the flight they booked.

grounding: A warden notes a student who fears flying after dramatic coverage but rides her scooter without a helmet.

Tuesday

Didn't go to the pool with Dolma again. There was this news story about a rare brain infection someone got from a lake in another state and I watched every video about it. Now every time I think of water, I think of that.

Dolma said, "Rafiq, there's been one case, and it was a lake, not a pool." I said, one is enough.

Then she said something that stuck. She said, "You rode here without a helmet. On the highway."

I laughed. But she didn't.

She's right, though. My cousin broke his wrist on a bike last year. Two boys from my college had scooter accidents this term. Nobody makes videos about those. They're too normal.

So I'm scared of a one-in-a-million thing and not scared of the thing that actually happens around me all the time.

Bought a helmet tonight. Still not sure about the pool. But the helmet, yes.

qa.q: What did Rafiq buy tonight?
qa.a: Bought a helmet tonight.

qa.q: Why was Rafiq more afraid of the rare infection than of riding without a helmet?
qa.a: Rafiq felt frightened because the rare case was dramatic and endlessly covered, while bike accidents felt too normal to worry about.

qa.q: Which of Rafiq's choices was the wisest, and why?
qa.a: Buying the helmet was wisest, because it protects against a danger that actually happens often around Rafiq.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt when Rafiq laughed about the helmet?
qa.a: Dolma probably felt worried and a bit frustrated, which is why she didn't laugh along.

grounding: A student fears a rare illness after dramatic news but rides without a helmet, until a friend points out the everyday risk.

The baby had been crying for an hour, the power was out in the Lucknow flat, and Tushar's phone buzzed nonstop: the family chat group. Jasleen's aunt had forwarded a message about child-kidnappers dressed as balloon sellers in the city. Within minutes, eight relatives had replied in panic. "Don't take the baby out!" "Lock all doors!"

Tushar, bouncing his daughter in the dark, read it twice. He looked around by torchlight. The bucket of water in the bathroom, full to the brim. Jasleen's mother's pills on the low table. The balcony railing with a gap wide enough for a small child.

He typed: "Has anyone checked if this is true? What do the police say?" He searched. The city police had called the message fake that same morning.

He posted the link. Then he emptied the bucket, moved the pills to the top shelf, and made a note to buy a railing net. Jasleen watched him, surprised.

The monsoon had made the ghat road slippery, and on Monday a private bus had gone off the edge near Mahabaleshwar. The photos were everywhere in Parul's village.

Parul taught at a school in the next town and took the government bus down that ghat every day. On Tuesday morning she stood at the bus stop, feeling sick.

Her neighbour Disha, sweeping the step, said, "You're not going?"

"Four years."

Parul took out her phone and paused. Before deciding anything, she looked for real information. The district transport office had posted figures: that road carried hundreds of buses a day, and serious accidents were rare, mostly private buses in heavy rain at night.

She let out a breath. "The government bus runs by day, with the same driver for years."

When it came, she got on.

In late November, the neighbourhood group chat in Lisbon lit up: a flat two streets away had been burgled, with photos of a smashed door. By evening, thirty messages. Someone posted an advert for an expensive alarm system.

Priscila felt her stomach tighten. She looked at her own door, the flimsy lock. She and Tomas had lived there three years. She had the alarm company's page open before she stopped.

"Wait," she said to Tomas. "Before I spend money out of fear, let me check."

She found the city police's yearly figures for their district. Burglaries had actually gone down over three years. Most happened when doors were left unlocked or windows open on the ground floor.

"We're on the fourth floor," Tomas said.

"And we never double-lock the door."

They didn't buy the alarm. Instead, Tomas fixed the old deadbolt that evening, and Priscila added a note by the door: "Double lock."

Dear Diary,
Winter camp, day 2.

Today we got teams for the camp quiz. My team has Santosh and a boy called Nirav.

Nirav is quiet and has thick glasses and reads all the time. I thought YES, he'll know everything. Santosh never stops talking and jumps around. I thought, oh no.

Then the quiz started. Nirav didn't know the capital of Australia. Santosh knew almost everything! Planets, cricket scores, old kings. He got us seven points alone.

At dinner I told Santosh I thought he'd be bad. He laughed and said everyone thinks that because he's loud.

I felt bad. I only looked at their faces and decided.

Tomorrow is the treasure hunt. I'm not guessing anymore.

Gautam

It was the last week before Christmas in Madrid, and the class was doing a times-table race for a box of turrón.

Camila looked around. Mateo, small and quiet, with glasses, sat perfectly still. Felix, who never stopped talking and got told off daily, was spinning his pencil.

Mateo will win, Camila decided. He looks like he knows maths. Felix is probably terrible.

The teacher called out: "Seven times eight!" Felix's hand shot up. "Fifty-six!" "Nine times six!" "Fifty-four!" Mateo got one.

Felix won the turrón.

"I'm not really good at times tables. I like drawing."

Camila bit into her piece of turrón. She had been so sure, just from his glasses.

On the first day of football trials in Bengaluru, Madhav watched the new boy, Jatin, walk onto the ground. Thin arms, glasses taped at the side, a science textbook still sticking out of his bag.

Madhav then pointed at another boy, broad and loud, laughing at the edge. "That one's the striker. Look at him."

Madhav stood with his mouth open.

After trials, Jatin said shyly that he'd played every evening in his old colony, usually against older boys.

Madhav felt stupid. He had picked the striker and the bookworm from their shapes and a textbook, and the field had shown him something completely different.

Twenty candidates in one day, a power cut at noon, and the generator fumes drifting into the interview room in Indore. Darshan was tired. So were the other two panel members.

By four o'clock he noticed a pattern. Pooja kept saying, "This one reminds me of Karthik," the best engineer they'd hired last year. Those candidates got high scores. A woman from a small college who'd answered every technical question well got "not quite our type". A man who spoke softly got "lacks presence".

During the tea break, he pulled out a sheet. "For the last six, can we try something? Same five questions for everyone. Each of us scores each answer from one to five, separately, before discussing."

Pooja frowned. "That's slow."

"It's fairer. And we'll know why we picked someone."

They tried it. The woman from the small college came out on top.

qa.a: Darshan felt tired and uneasy, noticing the panel was scoring people by resemblance rather than by their answers.

qa.a: Darshan proposed the same five questions for all and separate scores of one to five before discussion, so people are judged on evidence, not resemblance.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when the woman from the small college came out on top?
qa.a: Pooja might feel surprised and a little uncomfortable, realising the comparisons to Karthik had been steering her.

Farhan had been sitting on hiring panels at the Mumbai bank for two years before he noticed it.

Every candidate who had studied at the same college as the branch head, played cricket, and spoke with a certain confidence got through. The ones who looked or sounded different, a woman with a strong Bihari accent, a man in a wheelchair, a shy man who stammered at first, rarely did, however well they answered.

Then his colleague Amandeep mentioned during lunch, "That last candidate reminded me so much of our top performer." Farhan realised that was the whole method.

He went to the branch head with a proposal: every panel would use the same questions, scored separately on a written sheet, with notes explaining each score. No discussion until all scores were in.

In the next hiring round, four of the eight new joiners came from backgrounds the old panels had quietly passed over.

qa.a: That candidate would likely feel judged more fairly, on answers rather than accent.
